metadata.title: Decoding Singapore’s Mathematics Mastery: Student and School Predictors of PISA 2022 Performance
metadata.venue: Can. J. Sci. Math. Techn. Educ.

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for Singapore (15-year-old students) and applies the sampling weights provided in the PISA dataset to account for the complex two-stage stratified design (schools selected with probability proportional to size, then students sampled within schools). The authors state that these weights adjust for selection probabilities to support representativeness of the broader student population in Singapore. Plausible values for mathematics performance are also used to reflect uncertainty in the latent achievement measurement. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so variance estimation is described through the plausible-values aggregation approach rather than explicit replicate-weight procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 Singapore data and restricted the analytic dataset to Singaporean students and their school principals who participated in the mathematics assessment. The study reports a final dataset of 6,482 students from 157 schools. Missing data were handled via list-wise deletion (cases with missing values on analysis variables were removed). No additional grade or school-type restrictions beyond the PISA target population (15-year-olds) are described.

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics performance (Plausible Values; Rubin’s rules mean estimate)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel model (HLM/MLM) with plausible values: ICC intercept-only = 0.3049; full-model intercept = 528.60 (SE not reported in table excerpt). Variance explained: 64.25% of between-school variance and 26.04% of within-school variance explained by predictors. Table 2 reports mean estimates and significance via mean t-values (e.g., DISCLIM mean estimate 9.66, t=8.28, p<.001; EXPO21ST mean estimate 3.45, t=2.77, p<.001; MATHEFF mean estimate 28.61, t=23.63, p<.001; FAMCON mean estimate 12.42, t=16.28, p<.001; SC018Q01TA01 mean estimate 0.25, t=2.70, p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Singapore) mathematics literacy the study leveraged disciplinary climate in math (DISCLIM), exposure to reasoning/21st-century tasks (EXPO21ST), math self-efficacy (MATHEFF), familiarity with math concepts (FAMCON), and teachers’ full-time totals (SC018Q01TA01) to model mathematics performance (PVs combined with Rubin’s rules), finding that classroom disciplinary climate, reasoning/21st-century task exposure, and math self-efficacy were significant positive predictors while several reasoning/21st-century-oriented cognitive activation and self-efficacy components showed negative coefficients. This indicates that Singapore’s mathematics success is strongly associated with supportive classroom conditions and strong student confidence in core mathematics, but that simply increasing cognitively demanding reasoning tasks may require careful scaffolding to avoid performance declines.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2022 microdata for Singapore (6,482 students from 157 schools) to explain mathematics literacy performance using a two-level hierarchical linear model with student-level and school-level predictors. The authors apply PISA sampling weights and handle missing data via list-wise deletion, while mathematics achievement is represented through plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules across the ten PVs. The intercept-only model shows an ICC of 0.3049, indicating substantial between-school variance; in the full model, between-school variance drops from 3190.6 to 1135 and the model explains 64.25% of between-school variance and 26.04% of within-school variance. Significant positive predictors include DISCLIM, EXPO21ST, MATHEFF, FAMCON, and teachers’ full-time totals, whereas some reasoning-focused cognitive activation and reasoning/21st-century self-efficacy coefficients are negative. Limitations include reliance on self-reported questionnaire measures and the fact that the analysis is multilevel modeling rather than machine-learning prediction, so ML-specific claims about “best models” and predictive accuracy are not applicable.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the manuscript describes a multi-level modeling approach and plausible-values aggregation, it does not train or evaluate any machine-learning predictive algorithms (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM). Therefore, ml_techniques are intentionally left empty and primary is null, and the study is classified as exploratory multilevel analysis rather than an ML predictive paper.
